description: Chart 11 — Statewide overview of where venues sit against the transport network. Train + tram ROUTES (where public transport runs) are drawn over the full mesh of ~31,170 PT STOPS (where you can get on), with venues shown as precomputed hexagonal density cells (~8 km, built offline by tools/build-hexbins-victoria.mjs). This is a proximity/context map, not a service map — lines show where routes go and dots show where stops are, never when or how often services run. Full-width and tall so Victoria fills the frame and the route skeleton is legible. Data: venue_hexbins_victoria.topojson (from venues_web.csv); transport_stops_web.csv as stop points; pt_routes_simplified.topojson as lines; sa2_summary_simplified.topojson as the base.

subtitle: Venue density, stops, and train/tram routes in one statewide frame.
Proximity, not service frequency.

layer.description: Base: SA2 boundaries for geographic context (same base as the venue map).

Bus stops in Victoria (METRO BUS, REGIONAL BUS and SKYBUS), drawn as a faint neutral mesh so the dots read as texture showing how dense the bus network is — the 'where you can get on by bus' layer beneath the rail/tram skeleton. Filtered to bus modes only; identified in the legend rather than on hover.

Venue density across Victoria as precomputed hexagonal bins (~8 km cells). Each hexagon is a real geographic polygon built offline by tools/build-hexbins-victoria.mjs, so cells tile seamlessly under the conicEqualArea projection without any in-spec transform. Color encodes venue count per cell on a sqrt scale so both dense metro clusters and smaller regional nodes read clearly.

Train and tram routes as lines — the legible backbone of where public transport runs, drawn over the venue density layer. Direction/express variants collapsed to one feature per route; bus routes are intentionally not drawn (they would be spaghetti and blow the data budget) and are represented by the stop mesh instead.
